Lesson Overview

In this activity, you will launch your very own Creationeering™ vehicle company. You will build a real business identity from the ground up — naming your company, writing a mission statement, assigning leadership roles, mapping out your team structure, and defining what success looks like. Every great product starts before anyone picks up a single tool. It starts with a plan, a purpose, and a team that knows its role.

Learning Objectives

Students will:

  • Establish a formal company name and mission statement grounded in stewardship.
  • Assign and define leadership roles tied to the Engineering Lifecycle.
  • Create an organizational chart showing team hierarchy and information flow.
  • Map project milestones on a Gantt chart and identify the Critical Path.
  • Define measurable success metrics for their vehicle company.

items.definition: A short, clear declaration of a company's purpose, values, and commitment to its customers and community.
A diagram showing the hierarchy and reporting relationships within a company or team.
A visual timeline that maps out project tasks, their duration, and the order in which they must be completed.
The sequence of essential tasks that must be completed on time for an entire project to finish by its deadline.
The responsible management of resources — including time, talent, and money — on behalf of God and others.
Specific, measurable goals used to evaluate whether a project or company has achieved what it set out to do.

data.html:
Company Identity and Mission

Every great company starts with a "North Star" — a guiding purpose that shapes every decision. Before your first prototype is drawn, before a single spring is loaded, your team needs to know why you exist and who you serve.

That North Star is your mission statement. It tells your customers what they can expect from you, tells your community how you will treat the world around you, and reminds your own team what they are working toward when things get hard.

Think of it like the blueprint before the blueprint. An engineer never starts cutting without a plan — and a company never starts building without a mission.

Part 1 — Your Company Identity

  • Company Name: Choose a name that reflects your team's values and the kind of product you are building. It should be memorable and professional.
  • Mission Statement: Write 2–3 sentences that describe your obligation to your customers (quality and safety) and your community (service and stewardship).
    Example: "To provide innovative, high-performance kinetic transport solutions while honoring our resources through sustainable design and ethical craftsmanship."

Proverbs 29:18 says, "Where there is no vision, the people perish." A mission statement is your team's vision written down. It keeps everyone moving in the same direction — especially when the design gets complicated or the deadline gets tight.

Leadership Roles

A vehicle does not build itself — and neither does a company run itself. Every successful team needs people who own specific responsibilities. When everyone knows their role, the whole system works. When no one does, the whole thing stalls.

Your team will assign one member to each of the five key positions below. Each role is one "pillar" of the Engineering Lifecycle — take one pillar away, and the structure weakens.

Part 2 — Assign Your Team Roles

  • CEO — Oversees the entire project, ensures deadlines are met, and leads team meetings. The CEO keeps the big picture in view at all times.
  • Chief Engineer — Manages the design, testing, and technical integrity of the vehicle. If something breaks, this person finds out why.
  • Head of Sales — Responsible for marketing the vehicle and communicating its value to customers. This person answers the question: "Why should anyone care about what we built?"
  • Finance Manager — Tracks the budget, manages resource costs, and ensures financial stewardship. Every scrap of wood and every spring has a cost.
  • Legal Officer — Ensures compliance with project rules, safety standards, and ethical guidelines. This person makes sure the team plays fair and builds responsibly.

data.caption: A clean, simple five-box organizational chart showing CEO at the top, with Chief Engineer, Head of Sales, Finance Manager, and Legal Officer each in their own box directly below — connected by lines showing they all report to the CEO.

data.html:
Management Structure and Execution

Knowing your roles is step one. Step two is understanding how your team communicates and how long every task will take. This is where engineering thinking meets business planning.

An organizational chart shows who reports to whom — the chain of command that keeps decisions moving in the right direction. A Gantt chart shows what needs to happen and when — turning your project from a vague idea into a concrete schedule.

Together, these two tools are how professional engineers and project managers keep complex builds on track. You will use both.

Part 3A — Organizational Chart

Draw a simple diagram showing the hierarchy of your team and how information flows between roles. Who does each person report to? Who do they coordinate with? Use boxes and arrows — clarity matters more than artwork.

Part 3B — Production Gantt Chart and the Critical Path

List the major milestones of your vehicle project and map them on a timeline:

  • Design — Sketching and finalizing your vehicle concept.
  • Prototype — Building the first working version.
  • Testing — Running trials and recording performance data.
  • Final Build — Making improvements and completing the finished vehicle.
  • Marketing — Preparing your pitch and presentation materials.

Once your timeline is mapped, identify your Critical Path — the specific tasks that, if delayed, will push back everything else. Not every task is equal. Some can slip a day without consequence. Others cannot slip at all.

As you plan your schedule, think about the Three Ts of Stewardship: Time (are your deadlines realistic?), Talent (is each person in the role that fits them best?), and Treasury (are you tracking every material and cost?). Managing all three well is what separates a good team from a great one.

data.caption: A sample Gantt chart showing five project milestones — Design, Prototype, Testing, Final Build, and Marketing — mapped across a two-week timeline with color-coded horizontal bars. The Critical Path tasks are highlighted in a distinct color.

data.html:
Defining Success

Here is a question every engineer and entrepreneur must answer before the work begins: How will you know when you have succeeded?

"We did our best" is not a metric. "We finished" is not a metric. Real success metrics are specific, measurable, and tied to the goals you set at the start. They let you look back honestly and say — did we hit it, or did we fall short? And if we fell short, exactly how far, and why?

Part 4 — Your Success Metrics

Define three specific goals for your vehicle company. Each goal should be clear enough that someone outside your team could look at your results and immediately know whether you achieved it.

  • Goal 1: A performance target for your vehicle (distance, speed, accuracy, or another measurable result).
  • Goal 2: A process or teamwork goal (staying on budget, meeting a deadline, distributing work fairly across roles).
  • Goal 3: A stewardship or impact goal (minimizing material waste, maintaining a safe build environment, or producing a professional marketing presentation).

Real engineering projects live and die by their specifications — the exact, measurable standards a design must meet. Your success metrics are your specifications. Writing vague goals now means you will have no honest way to evaluate your work later. Be specific. Be honest. Be bold.

data.title: Check Your Understanding
data.html:
Q: What is the difference between an organizational chart and a Gantt chart?
An organizational chart shows who is in charge of what and how information moves between people. A Gantt chart shows what tasks need to happen and in what order over time. One is about structure — the other is about schedule.

Q: Why does the Critical Path matter?
Because not every task has the same consequence if it is delayed. Tasks on the Critical Path are the ones that, if they slip, push your entire deadline back. Knowing which tasks those are lets you protect them — and plan for what to do if something goes wrong.

Q: How does stewardship connect to business planning?
Stewardship means managing your resources responsibly on behalf of God and others. In business, that means using your time, talent, and budget wisely — not just to make a good product, but to honor the people and the world around you through the process of making it.
